gloss: The four weeks leading up to Christmas, starting on the fourth Sunday before Christmas Day.
usage: Used in church and everyday talk about the run-up to Christmas.
examples: We usually put the tree up at the start of Advent.
The school's Advent service is next Thursday.

gloss: A calendar with a little door for each day of December up to Christmas, often hiding a chocolate.
usage: Bought for children (and many adults) and opened one door a day from 1 December.
pragmatic_note: Luxury 'grown-up' advent calendars of beauty products, gin or cheese are now a popular British gift.
examples: Have you opened today's door on your advent calendar?
The kids get a chocolate advent calendar every year.

gloss: The evening and day of 24 December, before Christmas Day.
usage: Used everywhere; many people finish work early and go to the pub or to midnight mass.
examples: We always go to my mum's on Christmas Eve.
The shops close early on Christmas Eve.

gloss: 25 December, the main day of Christmas celebration in the UK.
usage: A public holiday when almost everything closes, including most shops and public transport.
examples: Are you hosting Christmas Day this year?
There are no trains on Christmas Day.

gloss: 26 December, a public holiday in the UK known for sales, sport and leftovers.
usage: Used everywhere in the UK; it is a bank holiday with a full programme of football and racing.
pitfall: Nothing to do with the sport of boxing; the name comes from 'Christmas boxes' once given to servants and tradespeople.
examples: We're going for a long walk on Boxing Day.
The Boxing Day sales start at eight in the morning.

gloss: The traditional British name for the bearded gift-bringer at Christmas.
usage: Used alongside 'Santa'; 'Father Christmas' sounds slightly more traditional and British.
examples: Has Father Christmas been yet?
The children left a mince pie out for Father Christmas.

gloss: A decorated Christmas den in a shop or garden centre where children meet Father Christmas.
usage: Common in department stores, garden centres and school fairs in December.
examples: We took the little ones to Santa's grotto at the garden centre.
The grotto queue was forty minutes long.

gloss: A paper tube that two people pull apart with a bang, containing a paper hat, joke and small gift.
usage: A fixture of British Christmas dinner tables and office Christmas lunches.
pragmatic_note: Cracker jokes are meant to be terrible; groaning at them is part of the ritual.
pitfall: Not a biscuit or a firework; few Americans know the custom.
examples: Shall we pull the crackers before the turkey comes out?
I got a mini screwdriver in my cracker again.

gloss: The brightly coloured tissue-paper crown found inside a Christmas cracker and worn during dinner.
usage: Worn, often reluctantly, by everyone at the British Christmas table.
examples: Grandad fell asleep with his paper hat still on.
Come on, put your paper hat on like everyone else.

gloss: A small sweet pastry filled with spiced dried fruit, eaten through the Christmas season.
usage: Offered to guests, at carol services and in offices all through December.
pitfall: Modern mince pies contain no meat; 'mincemeat' here means the sweet fruit filling.
examples: Would you like a mince pie with your coffee?
I've had far too many mince pies this week.

gloss: A rich, dark steamed pudding of dried fruit and spices, served flaming with brandy on Christmas Day.
usage: Traditional end to Christmas dinner, often bought months in advance or made on 'Stir-up Sunday'.
pitfall: 'Pudding' here is a dense fruit dessert, not the creamy American pudding.
examples: Who's brave enough to set fire to the Christmas pudding?
Do you want custard or brandy butter with your Christmas pudding?

gloss: A rich fruit cake covered in marzipan and white icing, eaten over Christmas.
usage: Made or bought in late autumn and served in slices with tea to visitors.
examples: Mum's already fed the Christmas cake with brandy.
Would anyone like a slice of Christmas cake?

gloss: The main festive meal on Christmas Day, usually roast turkey with all the trimmings, eaten at midday or afternoon.
usage: Used for the meal whatever time it is eaten; many families eat it around two o'clock.
pitfall: In the UK 'dinner' can mean the midday meal, so 'Christmas dinner' is often eaten at lunchtime.
examples: Christmas dinner's at two, so don't be late.
Who's doing Christmas dinner this year?
collocations: Christmas dinner with all the trimmings

gloss: A knitted pullover with a festive design, worn for fun in December.
usage: Hugely popular in offices and schools, especially on the charity Christmas Jumper Day.
pitfall: Say 'jumper', not 'sweater'; in the UK the joke is affectionate, not 'ugly'.
examples: Friday is Christmas jumper day at work.
That's the loudest Christmas jumper I've ever seen.

gloss: A large sock hung up on Christmas Eve for Father Christmas to fill with small presents.
usage: Children hang them on the end of the bed or by the fireplace.
examples: The kids were up at five to open their stockings.
I always put a satsuma in the toe of the stocking.

gloss: A small, inexpensive present suitable for putting in a Christmas stocking.
usage: Used by shops and shoppers in the run-up to Christmas.
examples: These little torches make great stocking fillers.
I've still got a few stocking fillers to buy.

gloss: A gift exchange where each person anonymously buys a present for one randomly chosen colleague or friend.
usage: Very common in British offices, usually with a modest spending limit.
pragmatic_note: Gifts are expected to be cheap and light-hearted; anything expensive or personal can feel awkward.
examples: We're doing Secret Santa at work with a ten-pound limit.
Who did you get for Secret Santa?

gloss: An informal Christmas party, especially the annual office celebration.
usage: Colleagues talk about 'the work Christmas do' throughout December.
pitfall: Americans often say 'holiday party'; in the UK 'Christmas' is used freely in workplace contexts.
examples: Are you going to the Christmas do on Friday?
The Christmas do is at a hotel this year.

gloss: A greetings card sent to family, friends and colleagues at Christmas.
usage: Many Britons still send cards by post and display the ones they receive on shelves or strings.
examples: I need to write my Christmas cards this weekend.
The last posting date for Christmas cards is next week.

gloss: A real or artificial evergreen tree decorated with lights and ornaments at Christmas.
usage: Usually put up in early or mid December and taken down by Twelfth Night.
examples: We're getting a real Christmas tree this year.
When do you put your Christmas tree up?

gloss: Glittering strips of metallic decoration hung on Christmas trees and around rooms.
usage: Everyday word; some see heavy tinsel as fun, others as a bit tacky.
examples: The office is covered in tinsel already.
Can you pass me that gold tinsel?

gloss: A decorative ball hung on a Christmas tree.
usage: The standard British word for Christmas tree decorations of this shape.
pitfall: Americans usually say 'ornament'; Britons say 'bauble' for the ball shape.
examples: Careful, those glass baubles were my grandmother's.
The cat keeps knocking the baubles off the tree.

gloss: Strings of small electric lights used to decorate trees, windows and gardens.
usage: Used at Christmas and all year round for garden parties and bedrooms.
examples: Can you untangle the fairy lights?
The beer garden is strung with fairy lights.

gloss: A public event where a celebrity or local figure turns on a town's Christmas lights.
usage: A big local occasion in towns and cities across the UK in November.
examples: The Christmas lights switch-on is on Saturday evening.
Half the town turned up for the switch-on.

gloss: An outdoor festive market with wooden stalls selling gifts, mulled wine and hot food.
usage: Now a fixture of many British city centres from mid-November, inspired by German markets.
examples: Shall we meet at the Christmas market after work?
The Christmas market gets packed at weekends.

gloss: Red wine heated with spices, sugar and orange, served warm in winter.
usage: Served at Christmas markets, carol services and festive parties.
examples: They're serving mulled wine after the carol concert.
Fancy a mulled wine to warm up?

gloss: Singing Christmas carols, often door to door or in the street, sometimes to raise money for charity.
usage: Associated with churches, schools and charity groups in December.
pragmatic_note: It is polite to give carol singers a coin or two, especially if they are collecting for charity.
examples: The carol singers came round last night.
We're going carol singing for the hospice.

gloss: A church or school service of Christmas carols and Bible readings.
usage: Held in churches, schools and workplaces in the weeks before Christmas.
examples: The school carol service is in the cathedral this year.
We always go to the candlelit carol service.

gloss: A play acted by young children telling the story of Jesus's birth.
usage: A much-loved fixture of British primary schools and churches in December.
examples: She's playing a sheep in the nativity play.
I've taken the afternoon off for the nativity play.

gloss: An orange with a candle and red ribbon, used in a children's church service before Christmas.
usage: Familiar from Church of England and school services in Advent.
examples: The children made Christingles at Sunday school.
Are you going to the Christingle service?

gloss: A church service held late on Christmas Eve, starting around midnight.
usage: Attended by churchgoers and many occasional visitors on Christmas Eve.
examples: We go to midnight mass after the pub.
Midnight mass starts at half eleven at our church.

gloss: The Christmas and New Year period.
usage: Common in advertising, news and polite conversation.
pitfall: Americans often say 'the holidays'; Britons more readily say 'Christmas' or 'the festive season'.
examples: The office is closed over the festive season.
Are you doing anything nice over the festive season?

gloss: A common British Christmas greeting, used alongside 'Merry Christmas'.
usage: Both are used in the UK; 'Happy Christmas' is slightly more traditional and British-sounding.
examples: Happy Christmas, see you in the new year!
Have a happy Christmas, and thanks for everything.

gloss: The single at the top of the UK chart in Christmas week, a keenly watched contest.
usage: Reported in the media every December, with betting on who will win.
examples: Who do you think will get Christmas number one?
It was the Christmas number one the year I was born.

gloss: The monarch's broadcast to the nation and Commonwealth, shown on Christmas Day at three o'clock.
usage: Many families still watch it after Christmas dinner; often called 'the King's speech'.
pitfall: Not the same as the King's Speech at the State Opening of Parliament, which sets out government plans.
examples: We always watch the royal Christmas message at three.
Shall we put the King's speech on?

gloss: The big retail discounts that begin on 26 December.
usage: A long-standing shopping tradition, now largely online too.
examples: I got this coat in the Boxing Day sales.
The Boxing Day sales start online on Christmas Day now.

gloss: Shop discounts held after Christmas and through January.
usage: Traditional retail season in the UK.
examples: I'll wait for the January sales before buying a new sofa.
The January sales seem to start earlier every year.

gloss: The evening of 5 January, traditionally the end of Christmas, when decorations come down.
usage: Many households take down decorations by Twelfth Night to avoid bad luck.
pragmatic_note: People argue each year about whether Twelfth Night falls on 5 or 6 January.
examples: The tree has to come down by Twelfth Night.
It's bad luck to leave decorations up after Twelfth Night.

gloss: A pantomime: a comic, family musical show based on a fairy tale, staged around Christmas.
usage: A much-loved British winter tradition at local theatres; 'panto' is the everyday word.
pitfall: In British English 'pantomime' is not mime; it is loud, colourful theatre full of jokes and audience shouting.
examples: We're taking the kids to the panto on Boxing Day.
This year's panto is Cinderella.

gloss: The comic female character in a pantomime, traditionally played by a man in outrageous costume.
usage: A beloved stock character; well-known actors and comedians often take the role.
examples: The panto dame stole the show again.
He's played the dame at the Palace for twenty years.

gloss: The traditional shout from a pantomime audience warning a character of a villain behind them.
usage: Shouted by children and adults at pantos; also used jokingly in everyday life.
pragmatic_note: Joining in loudly is expected at a panto; staying silent marks you out as a first-timer.
examples: The whole audience was screaming 'He's behind you!'
Oh no it isn't! Oh yes it is!

gloss: The last Sunday before Advent, when families traditionally make their Christmas pudding.
usage: A traditional, slightly old-fashioned custom revived by food writers and the media.
examples: We make the pudding on Stir-up Sunday and everyone makes a wish.
Is it Stir-up Sunday already?

gloss: 31 December, celebrated with parties, fireworks and a countdown to midnight.
usage: Used everywhere; London's fireworks on the Thames are shown on television.
examples: What are you up to on New Year's Eve?
We watched the fireworks on telly on New Year's Eve.

gloss: 1 January, a bank holiday across the UK.
usage: Many people spend it recovering, walking or watching sport.
examples: We always go for a walk on the beach on New Year's Day.
Is the pub open on New Year's Day?

gloss: The Scottish celebration of New Year's Eve, with parties, street events and customs.
usage: Used in Scotland and across the UK for the Scottish New Year; 2 January is also a holiday there.
examples: We're going up to Edinburgh for Hogmanay.
Hogmanay is a bigger deal than Christmas for my Scottish relatives.

gloss: The Scottish and northern custom of being the first visitor after midnight at New Year, bringing gifts.
usage: Mostly practised in Scotland and northern England; traditionally the first-foot is a tall, dark man.
examples: My grandad always went first-footing with a lump of coal.
Who's going to be our first-foot this year?

gloss: The Scottish song by Robert Burns sung at midnight on New Year's Eve, with arms crossed.
usage: Sung across the UK at New Year and at the end of some gatherings.
examples: Everyone linked arms for Auld Lang Syne.
Nobody ever knows the words to Auld Lang Syne beyond the first verse.

gloss: A promise to yourself to improve some habit, made at the start of January.
usage: Common in small talk in January; usually discussed with self-deprecating humour.
examples: My New Year's resolution is to cycle to work.
Have you broken your resolutions already?

gloss: The challenge of giving up alcohol for the whole of January.
usage: Widely discussed in British offices and media each January.
examples: I'm doing Dry January, so I'll have a lime and soda.
How's Dry January going?

gloss: 25 January, when Scots and others celebrate the poet Robert Burns with haggis, whisky and poetry.
usage: Celebrated with a 'Burns supper' in Scotland and by Scottish societies worldwide.
pragmatic_note: The 'Address to a Haggis' is recited theatrically before the haggis is cut.
examples: We're having haggis, neeps and tatties for Burns Night.
The pub's doing a Burns Night ceilidh.

gloss: A Scottish or Irish social evening of traditional folk dancing, with a caller guiding the steps.
usage: Popular at Scottish weddings, Burns Nights and university events; pronounced 'KAY-lee'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'KAY-lee', not as spelt.
examples: We had a ceilidh at our wedding.
Don't worry, the caller teaches you the steps at a ceilidh.

gloss: An informal evening of traditional English group dancing led by a caller.
usage: Common at village halls, fundraisers and weddings; similar to a ceilidh.
examples: The village hall is holding a barn dance for the church roof.
Nobody knew the steps, but the barn dance was great fun.

gloss: Scottish outdoor events featuring caber tossing, piping, Highland dancing and athletics.
usage: Held in Scottish towns through the summer.
examples: We watched the caber toss at the Highland games.
The Braemar Highland games are in September.

gloss: A Shetland fire festival in January ending with the burning of a replica Viking longship.
usage: Held each January in Lerwick, Shetland; known across the UK from television coverage.
examples: Up Helly Aa ends with them setting fire to a Viking ship.
I'd love to see Up Helly Aa one day.

gloss: The everyday name for Shrove Tuesday, when people eat pancakes before Lent.
usage: Used much more often than 'Shrove Tuesday' in conversation, schools and shops.
pitfall: British pancakes are thin, like crêpes, and usually eaten with lemon and sugar rather than syrup.
examples: It's Pancake Day, so we're having pancakes for tea.
Lemon and sugar is the classic Pancake Day topping.

gloss: A traditional Shrove Tuesday race in which runners toss a pancake in a frying pan.
usage: Held in villages, schools and charities on Pancake Day; the race at Olney is famous.
examples: The vicar won the village pancake race.
You have to flip the pancake at the finish line.

gloss: The forty days before Easter when Christians traditionally give something up.
usage: Widely understood; even non-religious Britons talk about 'giving up chocolate for Lent'.
examples: I've given up crisps for Lent.
What are you giving up for Lent?

gloss: The UK's Mother's Day, falling on the fourth Sunday of Lent, in March or early April.
usage: Usually called 'Mother's Day' in shops and conversation; 'Mothering Sunday' is the traditional name.
pitfall: The UK date differs from the American Mother's Day in May, so check before sending a card.
examples: Mothering Sunday is earlier this year.
We're taking Mum out for lunch on Mother's Day.

gloss: The Friday before Easter, a bank holiday across the UK.
usage: Many people use the four-day Easter weekend for a short break.
examples: The office is closed on Good Friday.
We traditionally have hot cross buns on Good Friday.

gloss: The Monday after Easter Sunday, a bank holiday in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
usage: Often marked by traffic jams, DIY and garden-centre trips.
examples: Are you working on Easter Monday?
Easter Monday isn't a bank holiday in Scotland.

gloss: A spiced sweet bun with currants, marked with a cross, traditionally eaten at Easter.
usage: Eaten toasted with butter; now sold in supermarkets for months around Easter.
examples: Shall I toast you a hot cross bun?
Hot cross buns are in the shops already.

gloss: A light fruit cake with marzipan, topped with eleven marzipan balls, eaten at Easter.
usage: A traditional but less common Easter bake, often made at home.
examples: Gran makes a simnel cake every Easter.
The eleven balls on a simnel cake are the apostles.

gloss: A game in which children search for hidden chocolate eggs at Easter.
usage: Held in gardens, parks and National Trust properties over Easter weekend.
examples: The National Trust is running an Easter egg hunt.
We hid the eggs for the Easter egg hunt.

gloss: A hollow chocolate egg, often boxed, given as a present at Easter.
usage: Hugely popular; children may receive several large boxed eggs.
examples: The kids got far too many Easter eggs.
I've hidden my Easter egg from my brother.

gloss: A trick or hoax played on 1 April, or the person fooled by it.
usage: Pranks must traditionally be played before midday; newspapers often print a spoof story.
pragmatic_note: By British tradition, a prank played after midday makes the prankster the fool.
examples: That story about the Big Ben clock is surely an April Fool.
April Fool! Your car's fine.

gloss: 1 March, the national day of Wales, marked with daffodils, leeks and Welsh costume.
usage: Celebrated in Welsh schools and by Welsh communities; not a bank holiday.
examples: The children wore daffodils for St David's Day.
Happy St David's Day to all our Welsh customers!

gloss: 17 March, the national day of Ireland, a bank holiday in Northern Ireland.
usage: Celebrated across the UK with parades and pub parties.
examples: The pubs are packed on St Patrick's Day.
St Patrick's Day is a bank holiday in Northern Ireland.

gloss: 23 April, the national day of England, named after its patron saint.
usage: Marked quietly compared with St Patrick's Day; not a bank holiday.
pragmatic_note: England's national day is low-key, and many English people are unsure of the date.
examples: Some pubs fly the St George's flag on St George's Day.
There's a St George's Day parade in town.

gloss: 30 November, the national day of Scotland.
usage: An official holiday in Scotland, though many people still work.
examples: There's a ceilidh on St Andrew's Day.
St Andrew's Day is Scotland's national day.

gloss: 1 May, a spring festival with maypoles and morris dancing; the first Monday in May is a bank holiday.
usage: Used both for the traditional festival and for the 'early May bank holiday'.
pitfall: Not the distress call 'Mayday' used by pilots and sailors.
examples: The village has maypole dancing on May Day.
Are you doing anything over the May Day bank holiday?

gloss: A tall decorated pole that dancers circle holding ribbons, weaving patterns on May Day.
usage: Found on village greens and in school May Day celebrations.
examples: The children danced round the maypole.
They put the maypole up on the green every spring.

gloss: Traditional English folk dancing by groups with bells, sticks and handkerchiefs.
usage: Seen at May Day, fêtes and folk festivals, often outside pubs.
pragmatic_note: Morris dancing is affectionately mocked as eccentric, but it has a devoted following.
examples: There's morris dancing outside the pub on Saturday.
My uncle does morris dancing every summer.

gloss: A girl crowned as queen of the May Day celebrations in a village or school.
usage: A traditional custom still found in some villages.
examples: My daughter was chosen as May Queen this year.
The May Queen leads the procession to the green.

gloss: The Christian festival of Pentecost; formerly a holiday, now replaced by the late May bank holiday.
usage: Mostly used by older people and churchgoers; 'Whit walks' survive in parts of the North.
examples: My nan still calls it the Whitsun bank holiday.
The Whit walks still happen in some Lancashire towns.

gloss: The period around the summer solstice in late June.
usage: Associated with long evenings, solstice gatherings at Stonehenge, and Shakespeare.
examples: Thousands gather at Stonehenge for midsummer.
It's light until ten around midsummer.

gloss: An autumn church and school celebration giving thanks for the harvest, with food donations.
usage: Held in schools and churches in September or October; tins often go to food banks.
examples: Can you send in a tin for the harvest festival?
The church was decorated for harvest festival.

gloss: 31 October, celebrated with costumes, pumpkins and trick-or-treating.
usage: Increasingly big in the UK, though many still see the American style as imported.
examples: Are the kids dressing up for Halloween?
We carve pumpkins every Halloween.

gloss: Children going door to door in costume at Halloween asking for sweets.
usage: Common in UK suburbs; a lit pumpkin often signals that a household is happy to take part.
pragmatic_note: Knocking at a house with no pumpkin or decorations is often seen as bad form.
examples: We took the kids trick-or-treating round the estate.
We ran out of sweets for the trick-or-treaters.

gloss: 5 November, when Britons mark the failed Gunpowder Plot of 1605 with bonfires and fireworks.
usage: Used across Britain; public firework displays are held on the nearest weekend.
pragmatic_note: The rhyme 'Remember, remember, the fifth of November' is known by almost every British child.
examples: Are you going to the fireworks on Bonfire Night?
The dog hates Bonfire Night.

gloss: The Gunpowder Plot conspirator whose arrest in 1605 is remembered on Bonfire Night.
usage: Used in the name 'Guy Fawkes Night' and in history lessons.
examples: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding the gunpowder.
We learnt about Guy Fawkes at school.

gloss: A stuffed effigy of Guy Fawkes burnt on top of a Bonfire Night bonfire.
usage: Once made by children who asked for 'a penny for the guy'; this custom is now rare.
examples: The kids made a guy out of old clothes.
They put the guy on top of the bonfire.

gloss: A large outdoor fire, especially one lit on Bonfire Night or to burn garden waste.
usage: Used for both festive fires and garden fires.
examples: They're building a huge bonfire on the rec.
Please don't have a bonfire while my washing's out.

gloss: A hand-held firework that burns with bright sparks, waved around on Bonfire Night.
usage: Given to children at Bonfire Night displays and used at weddings.
examples: Always wear gloves when you hold a sparkler.
We wrote our names in the air with sparklers.

gloss: An organised public show of fireworks, especially around 5 November.
usage: Local councils, schools and rugby clubs run displays near Bonfire Night.
examples: The rugby club's firework display is on Saturday.
Tickets for the firework display sold out.

gloss: An apple on a stick coated in hard, glossy toffee, eaten at Bonfire Night and fairs.
usage: Associated with autumn, Halloween, Bonfire Night and funfairs.
examples: I nearly lost a tooth on that toffee apple.
We had toffee apples by the bonfire.

gloss: The Sunday nearest 11 November, when the UK honours those who died in war.
usage: Marked by services at war memorials, wreath-laying and a national ceremony at the Cenotaph.
examples: There's a service at the war memorial on Remembrance Sunday.
The scouts march to the church on Remembrance Sunday.

gloss: 11 November, the anniversary of the end of the First World War, marked with a silence at 11 a.m.
usage: Also called Remembrance Day; many workplaces pause for the silence.
examples: The whole office stood for the silence on Armistice Day.
Armistice Day is always on the eleventh.

gloss: A red paper or enamel flower worn in autumn to remember the war dead and raise money for veterans.
usage: Worn from late October to 11 November by many people, including all TV presenters.
pragmatic_note: Wearing a poppy is a strong public convention; not wearing one on television can attract criticism.
examples: I need to buy a poppy on the way in.
She wears her poppy on her left lapel.

gloss: A two minutes' pause at 11 a.m. on Armistice Day and Remembrance Sunday.
usage: Observed in workplaces, schools, shops and at sporting events.
examples: The station fell completely quiet for the two-minute silence.
We'll observe the two-minute silence at eleven.

gloss: The bugle call played at Remembrance services and military funerals.
usage: Played at war memorials before the silence on Remembrance Sunday.
examples: The Last Post always gives me goosebumps.
A bugler played the Last Post at the memorial.

gloss: The national war memorial in Whitehall, London, focus of the Remembrance Sunday ceremony.
usage: Seen on television each Remembrance Sunday; many towns also have local war memorials.
examples: The King laid a wreath at the Cenotaph.
We watched the Cenotaph service on telly.

gloss: A monument listing local people killed in war, found in most British towns and villages.
usage: The focus of local Remembrance services each November.
examples: My great-grandfather's name is on the village war memorial.
Wreaths were laid at the war memorial.

gloss: A ring of flowers or leaves, laid in remembrance or hung on a front door at Christmas.
usage: Used for both poppy wreaths at memorials and festive door wreaths.
examples: The mayor laid a wreath at the memorial.
I made a holly wreath for the front door.

gloss: The Hindu, Sikh and Jain festival of lights, widely celebrated in British cities in autumn.
usage: Leicester's Diwali celebrations are among the largest outside India.
examples: The Diwali lights in Leicester are spectacular.
Happy Diwali! Are you celebrating with family?

gloss: Either of the two main Muslim festivals, Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, celebrated widely in the UK.
usage: Familiar in British schools, workplaces and city celebrations.
examples: Eid Mubarak! Have a lovely day with your family.
Several colleagues are off for Eid next week.

gloss: Europe's largest street festival, a Caribbean carnival in west London on the August bank holiday weekend.
usage: Famous across the UK; held on the Sunday and Monday of the late August bank holiday.
examples: We're going to Notting Hill Carnival on the Monday.
The steel bands at Notting Hill Carnival are brilliant.

gloss: An annual LGBTQ+ festival and parade, held in many British towns and cities in summer.
usage: Used as 'Pride' or 'London Pride', 'Brighton Pride' and so on.
examples: Are you going to Pride this year?
The high street was full of rainbow flags for Pride.

gloss: A Gloucestershire tradition in which people chase a wheel of cheese down a very steep hill.
usage: Held at Cooper's Hill each spring bank holiday; often reported as a classic British eccentricity.
examples: Did you see the cheese rolling on the news?
Only the brave do the cheese rolling.

gloss: An old English custom of singing to orchards or door to door in midwinter, drinking warm cider.
usage: Revived in cider-making areas like Somerset and Herefordshire.
examples: We went wassailing in the orchard on Twelfth Night.
Wassailing is meant to bring a good apple harvest.

gloss: A Derbyshire and Peak District custom of decorating wells with pictures made of flower petals.
usage: Held in villages through the summer, mainly in Derbyshire.
examples: We drove round the villages to see the well dressings.
The well dressing took a week to make.

gloss: A Welsh festival of music, poetry and performance, often competitive.
usage: The National Eisteddfod is held each August, moving around Wales.
examples: She won the harp competition at the Eisteddfod.
The school Eisteddfod is on St David's Day.

gloss: The British monarch and their close relatives, who carry out public and ceremonial duties.
usage: Used in news and conversation; often shortened to 'the royals'.
examples: The Royal Family appeared on the balcony after the parade.
She's a big fan of the Royal Family.

gloss: Informal term for members of the Royal Family.
usage: Common in tabloid headlines and casual conversation.
examples: The royals are visiting the town next month.
My nan reads everything about the royals.

gloss: The king or queen who is head of state of the United Kingdom.
usage: Used in formal, legal and news contexts; the monarch's role is largely ceremonial.
examples: The monarch opens Parliament each year.
She was the longest-reigning monarch in British history.

gloss: The ceremony at Westminster Abbey in which a new monarch is crowned.
usage: Used about royal history and recent coronations; often marked with street parties.
examples: We had a street party for the coronation.
The coronation was watched by millions.

gloss: A celebration of a monarch's reign reaching a milestone such as 25, 50, 60 or 70 years.
usage: Marked with bank holidays, street parties, bunting and commemorative mugs.
examples: The village had a jubilee street party.
We've still got a mug from the Silver Jubilee.

gloss: A party where neighbours close a residential street and share food at long tables.
usage: Classic British way to celebrate royal occasions and VE Day anniversaries.
examples: The council closed the road for the street party.
Everyone brought a dish to the street party.

gloss: Strings of small triangular cloth or paper flags hung up for celebrations.
usage: Seen at fêtes, royal celebrations, weddings and garden parties.
examples: The whole high street was covered in bunting.
Can you help me put the bunting up?

gloss: The annual military parade in June marking the monarch's official birthday.
usage: Watched on television and by crowds in London; ends with a balcony appearance and flypast.
pitfall: 'Colour' here means a regimental flag, not a hue.
examples: We watched Trooping the Colour on the telly.
There's a flypast after Trooping the Colour.

gloss: The ceremony at Buckingham Palace in which one set of royal guards replaces another.
usage: A major tourist attraction in London.
examples: We got there early to see the Changing of the Guard.
The Changing of the Guard doesn't happen every day in winter.

gloss: The popular name for a Yeoman Warder, a ceremonial guard at the Tower of London.
usage: Used by tourists and Londoners alike; the official title is Yeoman Warder.
examples: The Beefeater gave us a brilliant tour of the Tower.
Beefeaters wear red and dark blue uniforms.

gloss: The British national anthem, with 'Queen' replacing 'King' when a queen reigns.
usage: Sung at state occasions, some sporting events and the Last Night of the Proms.
examples: Everyone stood for God Save the King.
The band played the national anthem before kick-off.

gloss: The national flag of the United Kingdom, combining the crosses of England, Scotland and Ireland.
usage: The everyday name; 'Union Flag' is the more formal term.
examples: The street was full of Union Jack bunting.
He wrapped himself in a Union Jack at the match.

gloss: The red cross on a white background that is the flag of England.
usage: Flown at football and rugby matches and on St George's Day.
examples: The pubs were full of St George's flags for the World Cup.
The church flies the St George's Cross.

gloss: The flag of Scotland, a white diagonal cross on a blue background.
usage: Used in Scotland and at Scottish sporting events.
examples: Fans were waving the Saltire at Murrayfield.
The Saltire is also called the St Andrew's Cross.

gloss: The twice-yearly list of people receiving knighthoods, MBEs, OBEs and other awards.
usage: Published at New Year and on the monarch's official birthday.
examples: Our headteacher got an MBE in the New Year Honours.
Have you seen who's on the honours list?

gloss: Officer of the Order of the British Empire, an honour awarded for distinguished service.
usage: Spoken as letters; recipients may put 'OBE' after their name.
examples: She was awarded an OBE for services to nursing.
He's got an OBE, but he never mentions it.

gloss: The honour that gives a man the title 'Sir' (or a woman the title 'Dame').
usage: Reported in the honours lists; 'he got a knighthood' is the usual phrase.
pitfall: Address a knight as 'Sir' plus first name, as in 'Sir Paul', never 'Sir' plus surname alone.
examples: He received a knighthood for services to music.
She was made a dame in the same year.

gloss: A mark showing that a company supplies goods to the royal household.
usage: Seen as a royal coat of arms on packaging, shop fronts and adverts.
examples: The jam has a royal warrant on the label.
Holding a royal warrant is a big deal for a small firm.

gloss: A formal afternoon party held in a large garden, especially those at Buckingham Palace.
usage: Used both for royal garden parties and for smart private summer events.
examples: My aunt was invited to a garden party at the Palace.
The vicarage garden party is next Saturday.

gloss: The Royal Family appearing together on the Buckingham Palace balcony after a major event.
usage: A familiar moment in coverage of royal weddings, jubilees and Trooping the Colour.
examples: Crowds waited hours for the balcony appearance.
The flypast came over during the balcony appearance.

gloss: A ceremonial flight of aircraft in formation over a parade or event.
usage: The Red Arrows' flypast is a highlight of royal and national celebrations.
pitfall: Americans usually say 'flyover', which in the UK means a road bridge.
examples: The Red Arrows did a flypast over the Mall.
We heard the flypast before we saw it.

gloss: The British name for association football, the country's most popular sport.
usage: Always 'football' in the UK; 'soccer' sounds American.
pitfall: Say 'football' in the UK; 'soccer' marks you as American.
examples: Are you watching the football tonight?
He plays football every Sunday morning.

gloss: Casual word for football.
usage: Used among friends and in some headlines; also spelt 'footy'.
examples: Fancy watching the footie down the pub?
There's footie on the telly all weekend.

gloss: A competitive game between two teams or players.
usage: The standard British word for a football, rugby, cricket or tennis fixture.
pitfall: Britons say 'match' where Americans often say 'game'.
examples: What time's the match on Saturday?
It was a cracking match.

gloss: The marked grass area on which football, rugby, hockey or cricket is played.
usage: The standard word in British sport; a cricket pitch is the central strip between the wickets.
pitfall: Britons say 'pitch', not 'field', for football and rugby.
examples: The pitch was waterlogged, so the match was called off.
Fans ran onto the pitch at the final whistle.

gloss: A sports club's home venue, including the pitch and stands.
usage: Used by fans for a club's home, especially an older stadium.
examples: The ground holds about twenty thousand.
We got to the ground just before kick-off.

gloss: Zero, used when giving sports scores.
usage: Standard in British football and rugby scores; 'two–nil', 'nil–nil'.
pitfall: Say 'two–nil', not 'two–zero' or 'two to nothing', when giving British football scores.
examples: We won two–nil.
It finished nil–nil, a pretty dull game.

gloss: A game that ends with both teams on the same score.
usage: The standard British word; 'they drew' is the verb.
pitfall: Americans say 'tie'; in British football 'tie' means a knockout match, as in 'cup tie'.
examples: It ended in a two–all draw.
A draw away from home is a decent result.

gloss: A sports match scheduled for a particular date.
usage: Used in football, rugby and cricket; 'the fixtures' come out each summer.
examples: The new season's fixtures were released today.
We've got a tough fixture away at Leeds.

gloss: The shirt, shorts and socks worn by a team.
usage: Used for sport and generally for the gear needed for an activity.
pitfall: Americans say 'uniform'; in the UK 'uniform' is for school or work.
examples: The club has launched its new home kit.
Don't forget your PE kit tomorrow.

gloss: A person who follows and supports a particular sports team.
usage: Common in British football; 'Who do you support?' is a standard question.
pitfall: Britons 'support' a team; the American 'root for' sounds odd in the UK.
examples: Thousands of supporters travelled to the final.
Who do you support?

gloss: A match played at the opponents' ground.
usage: Common in football and rugby talk; dedicated fans 'go to away games'.
examples: I go to most away games with my dad.
We've got three away games in a row.

gloss: A match played at a team's own ground.
usage: Used in all team sports.
examples: Our next home game is against Villa.
We've lost every home game this season.

gloss: A ticket covering all of a club's home matches for a season.
usage: A badge of loyalty among football fans; also used for commuter rail tickets.
examples: I've had a season ticket for fifteen years.
There's a waiting list for season tickets.

gloss: A match between two local rival teams.
usage: Used across British sport, as in 'the north London derby'; pronounced 'DAR-bee'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'DAR-bee' in British English, not 'DUR-bee'.
examples: The derby is the biggest game of the season.
Tickets for the derby sold out in minutes.

gloss: The start of a football or rugby match, or the time it starts.
usage: Used constantly in match talk: 'What time's kick-off?'
examples: Kick-off is at three.
We got there five minutes after kick-off.

gloss: The break between the two halves of a match.
usage: Used in football and rugby; also used for the half-time score.
examples: We were two–nil down at half-time.
Grab us a pie at half-time.

gloss: Extra minutes added at the end of each half to make up for stoppages.
usage: Also called 'stoppage time' or 'added time'.
examples: They scored in the last minute of injury time.
There'll be at least five minutes of injury time.

gloss: An additional period played when a knockout match is level at full time.
usage: Used in cup football; followed by penalties if still level.
examples: The final went to extra time.
They scored the winner in extra time.

gloss: A series of penalty kicks used to decide a drawn knockout match.
usage: England's mixed history in shoot-outs is a national talking point.
examples: England lost on penalties again.
I can't bear to watch a penalty shoot-out.

gloss: A goal accidentally scored by a player against their own team.
usage: Used in football and figuratively for a self-inflicted mistake.
examples: They went ahead through an own goal.
That policy was a bit of an own goal.

gloss: Three goals by one player in a single match; also three successes in a row.
usage: Used in football, cricket and generally.
examples: He scored a hat-trick in the first half.
That's a hat-trick of wins for the club.

gloss: A match in which a team concedes no goals.
usage: Used about goalkeepers and defences.
examples: The keeper's kept five clean sheets in a row.
We need a clean sheet on Saturday.

gloss: The ranked list of teams in a league by points.
usage: Discussed constantly by fans; 'top of the table', 'bottom of the table'.
examples: We're top of the league table at Christmas.
Have a look at the table.

gloss: Being moved down to a lower division after finishing near the bottom of a league.
usage: A key feature of British football, where clubs move up and down divisions.
pitfall: American leagues have no relegation, so the idea may need explaining.
examples: They're fighting relegation again this season.
Relegation would be a disaster for the club.

gloss: Moving up to a higher division after finishing near the top of a league.
usage: Used across English football and rugby leagues.
examples: They won promotion on the last day of the season.
Promotion to the Premier League is worth millions.

gloss: The top division of English football.
usage: Often shortened to 'the Prem'.
examples: They've been in the Premier League for ten years.
Premier League tickets are very expensive.

gloss: Football clubs below the professional leagues in England.
usage: Used affectionately about semi-professional and local clubs.
examples: I'd rather watch non-league football than pay Premier League prices.
A non-league side reached the third round.

gloss: England's oldest football knockout competition, open to hundreds of professional and amateur clubs.
usage: Famous for 'giant-killings'; the final is played at Wembley in May.
examples: They're through to the fourth round of the FA Cup.
The FA Cup final is at Wembley.

gloss: A shock victory by a small club over a much bigger one, especially in a cup.
usage: Strongly associated with the FA Cup.
examples: It was the giant-killing of the season.
Non-league giant-killers made the headlines.

gloss: A match in a knockout cup competition.
usage: Used in football commentary and fan talk.
examples: It's a tricky cup tie away from home.
The cup tie went to a replay.

gloss: Informal football with five players per team, usually on a small indoor or artificial pitch.
usage: A popular weekly activity for friends and colleagues.
examples: I play five-a-side every Tuesday after work.
Do you fancy joining our five-a-side team?

gloss: Amateur football played on Sunday mornings by local teams.
usage: Associated with muddy pitches, enthusiastic amateurs and hangovers.
examples: He plays Sunday league for a pub team.
It looked like a Sunday league tackle.

gloss: An expert, often a former player, who analyses sport on TV or radio.
usage: Used for sport and politics; 'the pundits' on football coverage.
examples: The pundits all got that prediction wrong.
He's a pundit on the football highlights show.

gloss: The periods in summer and January when football clubs can buy and sell players.
usage: A media obsession, with 'transfer deadline day' covered live.
examples: They need a striker before the transfer window shuts.
It's transfer deadline day tomorrow.

gloss: Informal word for a football manager, or the boss.
usage: Used by players, fans and jokingly at work.
examples: The gaffer wasn't happy at half-time.
Ask the gaffer if we can leave early.

gloss: Stepped standing areas at a football ground; by extension, ordinary fans.
usage: Used historically and for modern safe-standing areas.
examples: My dad used to stand on the terraces every week.
The chant spread round the terraces.

gloss: A long-running betting game predicting the results of football matches, especially draws.
usage: Now mostly associated with older generations.
examples: My grandad did the pools every week.
He checked the results for his pools coupon.

gloss: A bat-and-ball game between two teams of eleven, central to English summer culture.
usage: Played from village greens to Test matches between May and September.
pitfall: American speakers often know nothing about cricket; Indian speakers usually know it well but may use different terms.
examples: Do you fancy watching the cricket at Lord's?
He plays village cricket on Saturdays.

gloss: An international cricket match played over up to five days.
usage: The most prestigious form of cricket; 'the Test' for short.
examples: The first Test starts on Thursday at Lord's.
We've got tickets for day three of the Test.

gloss: The Test cricket series between England and Australia, played for a tiny urn.
usage: A huge national sporting event every couple of years.
examples: England need to win the last Test to regain the Ashes.
Are you staying up for the Ashes?

gloss: The three stumps and two bails a batter defends; also a dismissal, or the pitch itself.
usage: Used in all cricket talk: 'take a wicket', 'lose a wicket'.
examples: He took three wickets before lunch.
The wicket's very dry, so it'll help the spinners.

gloss: A set of six balls bowled by one bowler from one end in cricket.
usage: Basic cricket vocabulary.
examples: He bowled a brilliant over.
There are three overs left before tea.

gloss: A team's or player's turn at batting in cricket.
usage: Used with the same form for singular and plural: 'one innings', 'two innings'.
pitfall: 'Innings' is singular in British English; baseball's 'inning' is different.
examples: What a fantastic innings!
England were all out for 200 in their first innings.

gloss: Dismissed as a whole team, so the batting innings ends; also 'all out'.
usage: Used in cricket reports and commentary.
examples: They were bowled out for 150.
England were all out just after tea.

gloss: The player batting in cricket; 'batsman' is the older term.
usage: 'Batter' is now the official term; 'batsman' is still widely heard.
examples: She's the best batter in the county side.
The batter was caught on the boundary.

gloss: The player who delivers the ball to the batter in cricket.
usage: Also the name of a hard round felt hat.
pitfall: In cricket you 'bowl', never 'pitch' or 'throw', the ball.
examples: Their fast bowler is lightning quick.
The spin bowler came on after lunch.

gloss: A score of one hundred runs or more by a single batter in an innings.
usage: Used across cricket; also called 'a ton'.
examples: She scored a century on her debut.
He's two runs short of his century.

gloss: A score of zero by a batter in cricket.
usage: Used in cricket commentary and humorously elsewhere.
examples: He was out for a duck again.
Out first ball for a golden duck.

gloss: Leg before wicket: a dismissal when the ball hits the batter's leg in line with the stumps.
usage: Spoken as letters; often hotly disputed.
examples: He was given out LBW.
That looked plumb LBW to me.

gloss: The shout ('How's that?') a cricket fielder makes to appeal to the umpire for a dismissal.
usage: Shouted on the field; also known from television commentary.
examples: The whole team went up shouting 'Howzat!'
The bowler appealed, but the umpire said not out.

gloss: The three upright posts of a cricket wicket; also the end of a day's play.
usage: 'At stumps' means at the close of play.
examples: England were 250 for three at stumps.
The ball clipped the off stump.

gloss: The painted line in front of the stumps where the batter stands.
usage: Used in commentary: 'at the crease', 'out of the crease'.
examples: The new batter is at the crease.
He was well out of his crease.

gloss: The break taken in the afternoon of a cricket match, traditionally for tea and cake.
usage: A cherished part of village and Test cricket alike.
examples: Play resumes after the tea interval.
The cricket teas at our club are legendary.

gloss: Interruption of a cricket match by rain; also used jokingly for any plan ruined by weather.
usage: A familiar phrase of the English summer.
examples: Rain stopped play just after lunch.
We were going to have a barbecue, but rain stopped play.

gloss: Amateur cricket played by village teams, often on the village green.
usage: A symbol of a traditional English summer.
examples: We watched village cricket with a pint in hand.
He's played village cricket for thirty years.

gloss: Professional domestic cricket played by English and Welsh county teams.
usage: Followed devotedly by a loyal, often older, audience.
examples: He plays county cricket for Yorkshire.
County cricket is quieter but very relaxing to watch.

gloss: The famous cricket ground in north London, known as 'the home of cricket'.
usage: Used about Tests and major matches; a pilgrimage for fans.
examples: We've got tickets for the Test at Lord's.
Lord's is the home of cricket.

gloss: A team sport with an oval ball that is carried and kicked; union and league are separate codes.
usage: Union is more associated with the South, Wales and private schools; league with northern England.
pragmatic_note: Rugby league and rugby union have different class and regional associations in England.
examples: Are you watching the rugby this afternoon?
He played rugby at university.

gloss: In rugby, a score made by grounding the ball over the opponents' goal line.
usage: Basic rugby vocabulary; worth five points in union.
pitfall: Rugby players score a 'try', not a 'touchdown'.
examples: Wales scored a brilliant try in the corner.
That's his third try of the season.

gloss: A rugby set piece where the forwards bind together and push to win the ball.
usage: Used in rugby and for any disorderly crowd pushing forward.
examples: The referee awarded a scrum.
There was a scrum at the bar after the match.

gloss: The annual rugby union championship between England, Scotland, Wales, Ireland, France and Italy.
usage: Played every February and March; a big pub and television event.
examples: The Six Nations starts next weekend.
Wales against England is the big Six Nations game.

gloss: The trophy contested by England and Scotland in their annual rugby match.
usage: Mentioned whenever England play Scotland in the Six Nations.
examples: Scotland have won the Calcutta Cup again.
The Calcutta Cup match is always fierce.

gloss: A famous long-distance steeplechase horse race held at Aintree near Liverpool each April.
usage: Many people who never bet otherwise have a flutter or join an office sweepstake on it.
examples: Have you picked a horse for the Grand National?
Our office runs a Grand National sweepstake.

gloss: An office or family game where everyone draws a horse or team and the winner takes the pot.
usage: Common in British offices for the Grand National, World Cup and Euros.
examples: Are you in the World Cup sweepstake?
I drew Scotland in the office sweepstake.

gloss: A five-day horse-racing meeting in June, famous for its royal procession, formal dress and hats.
usage: A highlight of the summer 'social season'.
examples: She's bought a new hat for Royal Ascot.
The dress code at Royal Ascot is very strict.

gloss: A major four-day jump-racing meeting at Cheltenham in March.
usage: A huge event for racing fans and Irish visitors.
examples: Half the office is off to the Cheltenham Festival.
He won a fortune at Cheltenham.

gloss: A famous flat horse race for three-year-olds, run at Epsom each June.
usage: Pronounced 'DAR-bee'; the name gave us the word for a local football rivalry.
pitfall: Pronounced 'DAR-bee' in British English.
examples: Who's the favourite for the Derby?
We watched the Derby at a pub in Epsom.

gloss: A person or shop that takes bets, especially on sport and horse racing.
usage: Used in everyday speech; 'the bookies' also means a betting shop.
examples: I'll pop into the bookies and put a fiver on.
The bookies have England as favourites.

gloss: A small, casual bet.
usage: Used light-heartedly, especially about the Grand National.
examples: I only have a flutter on the National.
Fancy a flutter on the Derby?

gloss: A bet that pays out if the horse wins or finishes in the top few places.
usage: Standard British betting vocabulary.
examples: I put a fiver each way on it.
It's worth an each-way bet at those odds.

gloss: The tennis championship held every summer in south-west London, the oldest in the world.
usage: A 'Wimbledon fortnight' of strawberries, white kit and rain delays.
pragmatic_note: Queuing overnight for Wimbledon tickets is a celebrated British tradition with its own etiquette.
examples: Are you watching Wimbledon this afternoon?
We queued overnight for Wimbledon tickets.

gloss: The annual rowing race between Oxford and Cambridge universities on the Thames.
usage: Watched by crowds along the riverbank and on television each spring.
examples: We watched the Boat Race from a pub in Putney.
Did Oxford or Cambridge win the Boat Race?

gloss: Henley Royal Regatta, a prestigious rowing event and social occasion on the Thames each summer.
usage: Associated with blazers, boaters and Pimm's.
examples: We're going to Henley this weekend.
The dress code at Henley is jackets and ties.

gloss: The Open Championship, the oldest major golf tournament, held on British links courses.
usage: Called 'the Open' in the UK, never 'the British Open'.
pitfall: Britons call it 'the Open', not 'the British Open'.
examples: The Open is at St Andrews this year.
He won the Open at his first attempt.

gloss: A huge annual road race through London, known for charity runners in fancy dress.
usage: Many ordinary people run it to raise money for charity.
examples: She's running the London Marathon for a cancer charity.
We cheered the runners at mile twenty.

gloss: A free, timed five-kilometre run held in parks every Saturday morning.
usage: Hugely popular in the UK; people talk about 'doing parkrun'.
examples: I do parkrun every Saturday morning.
There's a parkrun in the park near us.

gloss: A game of throwing small pointed arrows at a round board, popular in pubs and on television.
usage: Played in pubs and watched on TV, especially around Christmas.
examples: Fancy a game of darts?
The darts on telly is brilliant at Christmas.

gloss: The maximum darts score with three throws, famously bellowed by the announcer.
usage: Instantly recognised from televised darts; often written '180'.
examples: One hundred and eighty!
He hit three treble twenties for a 180.

gloss: A cue sport played on a large green table with red and coloured balls.
usage: Popular on television; the World Championship is held in Sheffield each spring.
pitfall: Snooker is different from pool, which uses fewer, often numbered balls on a smaller table.
examples: Is the snooker on tonight?
Grandad watches the snooker all afternoon.

gloss: A cue game played on a smaller table than snooker, common in pubs.
usage: Pub pool usually uses red and yellow balls in Britain.
examples: Do you want a game of pool?
The pub has a pool table out the back.

gloss: A game of rolling heavy balls towards a small target ball on a flat green.
usage: Associated with older players and summer afternoons at local clubs.
pitfall: Not the same as tenpin bowling, which Britons call 'bowling'.
examples: My grandparents play bowls every Thursday.
The bowls club has a lovely green.

gloss: A bat-and-ball game similar to baseball, played mainly in schools and parks.
usage: Played at school and at summer picnics and office away days.
examples: We played rounders at the work picnic.
I haven't played rounders since school.

gloss: A fast passing game, similar to basketball but without dribbling, popular with women and girls.
usage: Widely played in schools and amateur leagues.
examples: She plays netball for the county.
Netball practice is on Wednesday evenings.

gloss: A children's autumn game of hitting a horse chestnut on a string against an opponent's.
usage: Collecting conkers is a classic British autumn pastime.
examples: The kids collected conkers in the park.
We used to play conkers in the playground.

gloss: A game of dropping sticks off one side of a bridge and seeing whose emerges first.
usage: Comes from Winnie-the-Pooh; played by families on country walks.
examples: Let's play Poohsticks off the bridge.
My stick won at Poohsticks!

gloss: A race in which runners balance an egg on a spoon.
usage: A classic school sports day and village fête event.
examples: She won the egg-and-spoon race at sports day.
There's a parents' egg-and-spoon race too.

gloss: A public house: a licensed venue serving drinks and often food, central to British social life.
usage: Used everywhere; 'going down the pub' is a basic social ritual.
pitfall: A British pub is a community place for all ages, not the same as an American bar or club.
examples: Shall we go to the pub after work?
The pub does a great Sunday lunch.

gloss: The pub nearest your home that you go to regularly.
usage: Used as a noun: 'my local', 'our local'.
pragmatic_note: Being a regular at your local is a mark of belonging in a village or neighbourhood.
examples: The Red Lion is our local.
Let's have a quick one at the local.

gloss: A set of drinks bought by one person for everyone in the group, taken in turns.
usage: The round system is a core pub custom; 'It's my round' means I'm buying.
pragmatic_note: Skipping your turn to buy a round is a serious social faux pas in British pubs.
examples: It's my round. What are you having?
Whose round is it?

gloss: The standard way to ask what drink someone wants when you are buying.
usage: Said at the bar when it is your round.
examples: Right, what are you having?
I'm getting them in. What are you having?

gloss: The final chance to buy a drink before a pub stops serving.
usage: Often announced by ringing a bell behind the bar.
pitfall: Americans say 'last call'.
examples: Last orders at the bar, please!
Quick, it's nearly last orders.

gloss: The traditional call by pub staff that serving has finished and customers must finish up.
usage: Often heard as 'Time, gentlemen, please' in older or traditional pubs.
examples: The landlord rang the bell and shouted 'Time, please!'
Come on, folks, time, please.

gloss: A measure of beer or cider (568 ml), the standard British serving size.
usage: Used everywhere: 'a pint of bitter', 'going for a pint'.
pitfall: A British pint (20 fl oz) is larger than a US pint (16 fl oz).
examples: Fancy a pint after work?
Can I have a pint of lager, please?

gloss: Half a pint of beer or cider.
usage: Used at the bar: 'a half of cider'.
examples: Just a half for me, I'm driving.
Can I get a half of bitter?

gloss: Beer mixed with lemonade, making a weaker, refreshing drink.
usage: Ordered in pubs, especially on hot days or by drivers.
pitfall: British 'lemonade' here is clear and fizzy, like Sprite, not cloudy American lemonade.
examples: I'll just have a shandy, it's so hot.
A pint of shandy, please.

gloss: The person who runs a pub; also a person who rents out property.
usage: In pub talk the landlord or landlady is the host who sets the tone.
examples: The landlord knows everyone by name.
Ask the landlady if they do food.

gloss: The people who serve drinks behind the bar in a pub.
usage: The general British term; 'barman' and 'barmaid' are older words.
pitfall: 'Bartender' is understood but sounds American in a British pub.
examples: The bar staff were really friendly.
They're short of bar staff tonight.

gloss: Ordering and paying for drinks at the counter, as is normal in British pubs.
usage: In most pubs you order at the bar rather than waiting for table service.
pragmatic_note: There is no formal queue at a pub bar, but staff and customers notice and respect who was there first.
examples: You have to order at the bar here.
I'll get these, I'm at the bar anyway.

gloss: An outdoor area at a pub with tables, used when the weather allows.
usage: Packed on the first warm day of the year.
examples: Let's sit in the beer garden while it's sunny.
Every beer garden in town was full.

gloss: A weekly general-knowledge quiz held in a pub, with teams competing for a prize.
usage: A popular midweek social activity.
examples: Are you coming to the pub quiz on Thursday?
We came second in the pub quiz again.

gloss: A pub or restaurant buffet where roast meat is carved to order, served with vegetables.
usage: Associated with Sunday lunch at chain pubs and hotels.
examples: Let's go to the carvery on Sunday.
The carvery does a huge plate for a reasonable price.

gloss: Simple, hearty food served in pubs.
usage: Used affectionately for dishes like pies, fish and chips and burgers.
examples: The pub grub there is really good.
Fancy some pub grub tonight?

gloss: A pub that serves high-quality, restaurant-style food.
usage: Used about upmarket pubs, often in towns and the countryside.
examples: It's more of a gastropub than a boozer now.
We had lunch at a lovely gastropub.

gloss: Informal word for a pub, especially a plain, traditional one.
usage: Said affectionately; avoid in formal settings.
examples: It's a proper old-fashioned boozer.
There's a decent boozer round the corner.

gloss: Traditional cask-conditioned beer served without added gas.
usage: Championed by enthusiasts; pubs advertise 'real ales' on hand pumps.
examples: This pub has six real ales on.
He's really into real ale.

gloss: A traditional English amber beer, usually served from the cask.
usage: Ordered as 'a pint of bitter'; associated with older drinkers and traditional pubs.
examples: A pint of best bitter, please.
My dad only drinks bitter.

gloss: A pale, fizzy, cold beer; the most popular kind of beer in the UK.
usage: Ordered by name or brand; 'a pint of lager'.
examples: Two pints of lager, please.
Do you have any lager on draught?

gloss: An alcoholic drink made from fermented apples.
usage: Associated with the West Country, but drunk everywhere, especially in summer.
pitfall: In the UK 'cider' is always alcoholic; American non-alcoholic 'cider' is apple juice here.
examples: I'll have a pint of cider.
Somerset is famous for its cider.

gloss: Beer served from a cask or keg, rather than from a bottle.
usage: Used in pubs: 'What have you got on draught?'
pitfall: British spelling is 'draught', pronounced 'draft'.
examples: What have you got on draught?
They've got a new IPA on draught.

gloss: Two measures of a spirit served in one glass.
usage: Ordered at the bar: 'a double gin and tonic'.
examples: A double whisky, please.
Is that a single or a double?

gloss: An evening spent drinking at several pubs in succession.
usage: Associated with students, stag dos and birthdays.
examples: We're doing a pub crawl for his birthday.
The pub crawl ended at about midnight.

gloss: When a pub closes its doors but lets regulars carry on drinking after hours.
usage: A semi-legendary, unofficial custom in some rural pubs.
examples: We ended up in a lock-in at the village pub.
The landlord's famous for his lock-ins.

gloss: A pub not tied to a particular brewery, so it can sell any beer.
usage: Often written on pub signs.
examples: It's a free house, so the beer selection changes.
The sign says 'Free House' above the door.

gloss: A small, cosy, private room in a traditional pub.
usage: Found in older pubs; often has a fire.
examples: Let's grab the snug, it's warmer.
The snug only fits about eight people.

gloss: The painted hanging board outside a pub showing its name and picture.
usage: A distinctive feature of British streets and villages.
examples: Look out for the pub sign with the red lion.
The old pub sign was repainted.

gloss: A coin-operated gambling machine found in pubs and amusement arcades.
usage: The usual British word for a slot machine.
examples: He put all his change in the fruit machine.
The fruit machine flashes in the corner.

gloss: A traditional pub game like bowling, knocking down nine wooden pins with a ball.
usage: Played in pub leagues, especially in the West Country.
examples: The pub has a skittle alley out the back.
We've got a skittles match on Friday.

gloss: Never drinking alcohol.
usage: Used neutrally; 'I'm teetotal' is a common, accepted answer in pubs.
examples: He's teetotal, so he'll have a lemonade.
I've been teetotal for years.

gloss: Said when clinking glasses before drinking; also an informal 'thank you' or 'goodbye'.
usage: Hugely common in Britain in all three senses.
pragmatic_note: Britons use 'cheers' as a casual thanks many times a day; it is not only a toast.
examples: Cheers, everyone, happy birthday!
Cheers for that, mate.

gloss: The British Broadcasting Corporation, the UK's public service broadcaster for television, radio and online.
usage: A national institution, often discussed in debates about funding and impartiality.
examples: It was on the BBC news this morning.
The BBC is funded by the licence fee.

gloss: Affectionate nickname for the BBC.
usage: Used informally and in newspaper headlines.
examples: Is it on the Beeb or ITV?
The Beeb has some great dramas this autumn.

gloss: The BBC's national speech radio station, broadcasting news, drama, comedy and documentaries.
usage: Strongly associated with the educated middle classes.
examples: I heard an interesting piece on Radio 4.
Radio 4 is always on in our kitchen.

gloss: The BBC's radio weather report for sea areas around the British Isles, famous for its hypnotic wording.
usage: Loved even by people who never go to sea; many find it soothing at night.
examples: I fall asleep listening to the Shipping Forecast.
Dogger, Fisher, German Bight... I love the Shipping Forecast.

gloss: The annual fee UK households pay for a TV licence, which funds the BBC.
usage: Debated constantly in politics and media.
pitfall: Spelt 'licence' as a noun in British English; 'license' is the verb.
examples: The licence fee funds the BBC.
Do you need a licence if you only watch catch-up?

gloss: Informal word for television.
usage: Used widely in casual speech by all classes.
examples: What's on telly tonight?
We just stayed in and watched telly.

gloss: A broadcast on television or radio.
usage: Standard British word and spelling.
pitfall: British spelling is 'programme' for broadcasts, but 'program' for computer software.
examples: Did you see that programme about bees?
It's my favourite programme.

gloss: A set of episodes of a TV programme broadcast in one run.
usage: Britons say 'the new series', where Americans say 'the new season'.
pitfall: 'Season' is spreading in the UK, but 'series' is still standard.
examples: The new series starts on Sunday.
Have you watched the second series?

gloss: A soap opera: a long-running TV drama about the everyday lives of a community.
usage: British soaps are broadcast several evenings a week and discussed widely.
pragmatic_note: British soaps are known for gritty, working-class settings rather than glamour.
examples: My mum never misses her soaps.
The soap had a big twist on Christmas Day.

gloss: A whole series of a TV programme available to watch in one go.
usage: Now mostly used for streaming; 'a box set binge'.
examples: We've been working our way through a box set.
It's a perfect box set for the winter.

gloss: A comedy programme in which celebrities answer questions or play games.
usage: A popular British TV format.
examples: He's on every panel show at the moment.
That panel show is hilarious.

gloss: A television programme in which a host interviews celebrity guests.
usage: The usual British term.
examples: She was on a chat show last night.
He's hosting a new chat show.

gloss: A situation comedy: a comic television series about recurring characters.
usage: Britain has a strong sitcom tradition, often built on awkwardness and failure.
examples: It's my favourite British sitcom.
They're making a new sitcom set in an office.

gloss: A television drama set in the past, often with grand houses and costumes.
usage: A popular British export, especially at Sunday evening teatime.
examples: There's a new period drama on Sunday nights.
I love a good period drama.

gloss: 9 p.m., after which UK television may show content unsuitable for children.
usage: Used in debates about broadcasting standards.
examples: That joke shouldn't have gone out before the watershed.
It's on after the watershed.

gloss: An advertisement on TV, radio or online.
usage: The usual British word; 'ad' is also common.
pragmatic_note: Supermarket Christmas adverts are an annual event that the media reviews like films.
examples: I'll make a tea during the adverts.
Have you seen the new Christmas advert?

gloss: A person who reads the news on television or radio.
usage: The traditional British term.
examples: She's a newsreader on the evening news.
The newsreader nearly laughed on air.

gloss: A person who introduces a TV or radio programme.
usage: Standard British term.
examples: He's a children's TV presenter.
The presenter interviewed the minister.

gloss: A popular newspaper with a smaller format, bold headlines and celebrity stories.
usage: Used about mass-market papers, often critically.
examples: It was all over the tabloids.
The tabloids love a royal story.

gloss: A serious, quality newspaper, traditionally printed on large pages.
usage: Used even though many such papers now print in smaller formats.
examples: He reads a broadsheet on the train.
The broadsheets covered the story in depth.

gloss: Weekly Sunday newspapers, often thick with supplements and magazines.
usage: Reading them leisurely is a traditional Sunday ritual.
examples: I like to read the Sunday papers in bed.
Can you pick up the Sunday papers?

gloss: A journalist who answers readers' letters about personal problems.
usage: Used about newspaper and magazine columns, and jokingly for a friend who gives advice.
examples: She writes to an agony aunt every week.
I'm the office agony aunt.

gloss: A crossword in which each clue is a word puzzle.
usage: A beloved ritual for many newspaper readers.
examples: He does the cryptic crossword every morning.
I only got three clues in the cryptic crossword.

gloss: A radio or TV programme in which listeners call to speak live.
usage: Common on local and talk radio.
examples: There's a phone-in about potholes on local radio.
She rang a radio phone-in.

gloss: The series of short beeps on BBC radio marking the exact hour.
usage: Known to all Radio 4 listeners as the cue for the news.
examples: The news starts after the pips.
I set my watch by the pips.

gloss: A one-off festive episode of a TV series broadcast at Christmas.
usage: Eagerly awaited each year by British viewers.
examples: The Christmas special is on straight after the royal Christmas message.
That sitcom's Christmas special was brilliant.

gloss: Light, fine rain falling steadily.
usage: A staple of British weather talk.
examples: It's only drizzle, you won't need a coat.
It drizzled all afternoon.

gloss: A mix of mist and drizzle.
usage: Regional, especially in the South West and Cornwall; many Britons will not know it.
examples: It's mizzling again down in Cornwall.
That fine mizzle soaks you through.

gloss: Raining very lightly, with just a few drops falling.
usage: Used in casual small talk.
examples: It's spitting a bit, take a brolly.
It's only spitting.

gloss: Raining very heavily.
usage: Very common in casual conversation; avoid in formal writing.
examples: It's absolutely chucking it down out there.
It chucked it down all weekend.

gloss: Raining heavily.
usage: Neutral, everyday phrase.
examples: It's pouring, I'll get a taxi.
It poured all day at the festival.

gloss: A sudden, very heavy fall of rain.
usage: Used in conversation and weather forecasts.
examples: We got caught in a downpour.
There could be heavy downpours later.

gloss: A short period of rain.
usage: Used constantly in British forecasts: 'sunshine and showers'.
examples: There'll be showers this afternoon.
Typical April: sunshine and showers.

gloss: Periods of sunshine between clouds.
usage: A classic phrase from British weather forecasts.
examples: Sunny spells and the odd shower this afternoon.
We had sunny spells most of the day.

gloss: Covered with cloud, so the sky is grey all over.
usage: Used in forecasts and conversation.
examples: It's overcast but dry.
The sky's been overcast all week.

gloss: Of the sky or weather: cloudy and dull.
usage: A very common description of a British day.
pitfall: British spelling is 'grey'.
examples: It's another grey day.
It's been grey since Sunday.

gloss: Of weather: warm, humid and airless.
usage: Common in British weather talk; pronounced with a soft 's'.
pitfall: Pronounced 'clohss' (like 'dose'), not 'clohz' like the verb 'close'.
examples: It's very close today, there'll be a storm later.
It's so close in here, open a window.

gloss: Unpleasantly warm and humid.
usage: Everyday weather word.
examples: It's really muggy this evening.
I can't sleep when it's this muggy.

gloss: Cold, especially sharply cold.
usage: Common in casual conversation.
examples: It's a bit nippy this morning.
Bring a jumper, it gets nippy in the evening.

gloss: Chilly.
usage: Informal, especially northern and Midlands.
examples: It's a bit parky out today.
Wrap up, it's parky.

gloss: Uncomfortably cool.
usage: Neutral, everyday weather word.
examples: It's a bit chilly for shorts.
It gets chilly once the sun goes down.

gloss: Of weather: cold and fresh in a way that feels invigorating.
usage: Often a humorous understatement for a cold, windy day at the seaside.
pragmatic_note: Calling icy wind 'bracing' is a classic piece of British stoicism.
examples: It was a bracing walk along the cliffs.
Bit bracing on the beach today.

gloss: Of weather: cool and slightly windy.
usage: Often understatement for cold and blustery.
pragmatic_note: 'A bit fresh' often means 'quite cold' in British understatement.
examples: It's a bit fresh this morning.
Fresh, but lovely and sunny.

gloss: Of weather: not as cold as expected for the season.
usage: Often used about winter.
examples: It's very mild for November.
We've had a mild winter so far.
collocations: mild for the time of year

gloss: A very hot day.
usage: Used in conversation and tabloid headlines.
examples: It's going to be a scorcher tomorrow.
Saturday was an absolute scorcher.

gloss: A spell of unusually hot weather.
usage: Hot spells cause much national comment and occasional hosepipe bans.
examples: The trains can't cope with the heatwave.
We're in the middle of a heatwave.

gloss: A temporary ban on using garden hoses during a drought.
usage: Announced by water companies in hot, dry summers.
examples: There's a hosepipe ban in the South East.
The lawn's gone brown since the hosepipe ban.

gloss: A short spell of very cold weather.
usage: Used in conversation and the news.
examples: There's a cold snap coming next week.
The cold snap froze the pipes.

gloss: A thin layer of ice crystals on surfaces after a freezing night.
usage: Used in forecasts and gardening talk.
examples: There was a hard frost last night.
I had to scrape the frost off the car.

gloss: Thin, nearly invisible ice on roads and pavements.
usage: Common in winter warnings.
examples: Watch out for black ice on the back roads.
I slipped on black ice this morning.

gloss: Rain mixed with snow or partly melted snow.
usage: Common in British winters, often instead of proper snow.
pitfall: In US English 'sleet' can mean ice pellets; in the UK it means wet, half-melted snow.
examples: It's more sleet than snow.
Sleet's forecast for the hills.

gloss: Windy, with strong gusts.
usage: Common in forecasts and small talk.
examples: It's a blustery day on the coast.
Hold on to your hat, it's blustery.

gloss: A very strong wind.
usage: Used in forecasts and the Shipping Forecast.
examples: Gales are forecast for the west coast.
It's blowing a gale out there.

gloss: An event or period ruined by rain.
usage: Used about summers, festivals and bank holidays.
examples: The bank holiday was a total washout.
Last summer was a washout.

gloss: A small-talk phrase meaning the weather has improved.
usage: Said casually to neighbours and colleagues.
examples: It's turned out nice again.
It's turned out nice for the fête.

gloss: The end of British Summer Time in late October, when clocks go back one hour.
usage: Marks the start of dark evenings and is widely discussed.
examples: The clocks go back this weekend.
It's dark by five now the clocks have gone back.

gloss: Days are getting shorter as autumn arrives.
usage: A classic piece of autumnal small talk.
examples: The nights are really drawing in now.
I hate it when the nights draw in.

gloss: An official yellow, amber or red alert issued by the Met Office for severe weather.
usage: Used in forecasts and news.
examples: There's an amber weather warning for snow.
A yellow warning for wind is in place.

gloss: A line of people waiting their turn.
usage: Queuing is a deeply ingrained British habit, from buses to bars.
pragmatic_note: Queue discipline is taken very seriously; disapproval is usually silent but intense.
examples: Is this the queue for tickets?
There's a huge queue at the post office.

gloss: To push in ahead of people already waiting.
usage: A serious breach of British etiquette.
examples: He tried to jump the queue at the bar.
Sorry, I think you've jumped the queue.

gloss: An apology word that Britons also use to excuse themselves, ask for repetition or soften a request.
usage: Said constantly, even when someone else is at fault.
pragmatic_note: Britons often say 'sorry' when someone bumps into them; it is politeness, not an admission.
examples: Sorry, could I just squeeze past?
Sorry, what was that?

gloss: A polite phrase used to get attention or to ask someone to move.
usage: Used with strangers, in shops and on public transport.
examples: Excuse me, is this seat taken?
Excuse me, could I get past?

gloss: A polite word asking someone to repeat what they said.
usage: Common and polite; in upper-middle-class circles 'Sorry?' or 'What?' is often preferred.
pragmatic_note: Whether to say 'pardon' or 'what?' has long been a marker in British class etiquette.
examples: Pardon? I didn't catch that.
I beg your pardon?

gloss: A polite phrase letting someone go first through a door or in a queue.
usage: Expected courtesy in British daily life.
examples: After you.
No, after you, please.

gloss: A stoic reply meaning 'I'm fine, all things considered'.
usage: Used in small talk, especially by older people.
pragmatic_note: It signals British stoicism: a modest 'fine', never enthusiasm.
examples: How are you? Oh, mustn't grumble.
Mustn't grumble, could be worse.

gloss: A standard, modest reply to 'How are you?'.
usage: Very common British reply, meaning roughly 'fine'.
